title: Webhooks and async APIs
subtitle: Webhooks arrive late, twice, out of order, or from someone pretending to be the sender. Here is how to build both ends so none of that hurts.

c.v: On 15 August 2023, at 16:58 UTC, an internal GitHub job queue started to fall behind. That queue processes

The cause was a large and lasting spike in webhook deliveries. Customers waited up to 4.5 hours for some webhooks. GitHub fixed it by blocking events from the sources of the extra load. Then the backlog drained slowly.
Think about what that means for a receiver. Your
bot or deploy tool waits for a push event. The event does not come for hours. Nothing is broken on your side, so no alert fires.
When the backlog drains, you could get hundreds of old events close together. Your handler must not run them all twice, run them in the wrong order, or fall over.
Webhooks fail in four ways: late, twice, out of order, and fake. This lesson shows how to build both ends so each failure is boring.

q.v: Your framework parses the JSON body and you compute the HMAC over the re-serialised object. Real Stripe events now fail the signature check. Why?

options.v: The bytes changed. The signature covers the raw body, so you must check it before any parsing.

why.v: Stripe needs the raw request body for verification, and any change to it makes verification fail.

q.v: A request has a valid Stripe signature, but its timestamp is two hours old. What should your endpoint do?

options.v: Accept it. The signature is valid.
Reject it. It may be a replayed copy, and real retries come with a fresh timestamp.

why.v: The timestamp is signed, so an attacker cannot change it. Stripe makes a new timestamp and signature for each retry.

q.v: Your endpoint gets invoice.paid before invoice.created for the same invoice. What is the best response?

options.v: Return 500, so the sender retries until the order is right.
Fetch the current invoice from the provider's API and act on that.
Drop the event. It arrived in the wrong order.

why.v: Stripe does not promise order and suggests using the API to get missing objects.

q.v: Your handler needs 20 seconds to do its work. GitHub waits about 10. What should you change?

options.v: Verify, save the event to a queue, and answer 2xx at once. A worker does the rest.
Ask users to raise GitHub's timeout.
Answer 2xx before you check the signature.

why.v: GitHub expects a 2xx within 10 seconds and suggests a queue to process payloads in the background.

q.v: A customer sets their webhook URL to an address that resolves to 169.254.169.254. What should your sender do?

options.v: Send it. The customer chose the URL.
Block it. Webhook calls must not reach internal or metadata addresses.
Send it, but without a signature.

why.v: This is SSRF. OWASP says attackers use it to steal credentials from cloud metadata services.
